key_terms.meaning: Digital money whose ownership is recorded on a shared ledger and proved by cryptographic keys, so no bank approves each payment.
A ledger copied across many nodes, updated by agreed rules, so no single party controls it.
Trying to spend the same digital coin more than once.
Software or device that stores keys, builds transactions and signs them; coins stay on the blockchain.
A native unit of value on a blockchain, such as bitcoin (BTC) on Bitcoin.
A digital asset issued on an existing blockchain, not the chain's native coin.
Private keys authorise spends; public keys and addresses receive funds.
An amount of bitcoin locked by a script; it becomes spendable as a UTXO until spent.
A fixed-size summary holding the previous block hash, Merkle root, time, difficulty target and nonce.
One hash committing to all transactions in a block, allowing compact proofs of inclusion.
Unspent Transaction Output; the set of spendable outputs that a transaction consumes and replaces.
A small stack-based language that locks each output and is run to check a spend.
Pay-to-Public-Key-Hash; the common script that pays to a hash of the receiver's public key.
New bitcoin paid to the miner of a valid block; it halves about every 210,000 blocks.
Miners who combine hash power and share rewards to reduce income variance.
A block added after the block containing a transaction; more confirmations make reversal harder.
Each node's pool of valid unconfirmed transactions waiting to be mined.
A node that validates every transaction and block against the consensus rules.
An altcoin that stores name-value pairs on its blockchain, used for decentralised naming.
An altcoin offering shielded transactions that hide sender, receiver and amount.

takeaways: Cryptocurrency replaces per-payment bank approval with a shared ledger plus cryptographic proof of ownership.
A Bitcoin transaction spends earlier UTXOs and creates new outputs, while a block batches such transactions under one hash-linked header.
Bitcoin script is the lock on each output; a valid spend is a script run that leaves exactly TRUE.
Miners maximise expected revenue by choosing transactions and hash power after accounting for subsidy, fees and costs.
Waiting for confirmations makes double spending impractical because an attacker must overtake accumulated proof of work.
A wallet stores keys and signs transactions; the coins themselves remain unspent outputs on the blockchain.
Altcoins keep Bitcoin's core design but change one feature, such as Namecoin's naming registry or Zcash's shielded payments.
Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous: public transaction links plus off-chain data can reveal address ownership.
Bitcoin trades throughput and flexibility for security and decentralisation, so its limits are technical, economic and legal at once.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress Bitcoin transaction and block construction, script validation, mining rewards, confirmations and double-spending attacks, wallet key handling, altcoin trade-offs, privacy and Bitcoin's limits.

glossary.def: A short encoded form of a public key hash used to receive bitcoin.
A cryptocurrency that copies Bitcoin's core design but changes some feature.
A peer-to-peer cryptocurrency system whose ledger is maintained by proof-of-work mining.
A batch of transactions with a header that links it to the previous block.
A hash-linked chain of blocks that records agreed transaction history.
Keeping private keys offline so online attackers cannot reach them.
A measure of how hard it is to find a block hash below the target.
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, used by Bitcoin to sign transactions.
The amount a spender gives to the miner, equal to input value minus output value.
A function that maps data to a fixed-size fingerprint; Bitcoin uses SHA-256.
A wallet that derives many keys from one seed using a deterministic hierarchy.
A wallet connected to the internet, convenient but more exposed to attack.
A binary hash tree that summarises transactions and supports inclusion proofs.
Repeated hashing to find a valid block header under the proof-of-work target.
A header field miners change while searching for a valid proof-of-work hash.
A network where nodes connect directly and relay data without a central server.
A secret number that authorises spending from the corresponding public key.
A costly proof, found by hashing, that a block was produced with real effort.
A number derived from a private key, used to verify signatures and form addresses.
The pseudonymous author or authors of the original Bitcoin design.
Segregated Witness, a Bitcoin upgrade that moves witness data and fixes transaction malleability.
A lightweight client that checks proof-of-work headers and Merkle proofs, not all transactions.
Unspent transaction output, the spendable unit of bitcoin value.
Control of a majority of hash power, enough to reorg recent blocks and double spend.
